title: JavaScript
description: The language itself, from types and coercion through closures, this, prototypes and the event loop. Built around the output-prediction puzzles and concept questions that frontend interviews lean on.

chapters.title: Types, Values and Coercion
chapters.summary: The eight JavaScript types, how equality works, and the coercion rules behind the language's most famous surprises.

lesson.heading: Primitives and objects
lesson.body:
JavaScript has eight types. Seven are primitives: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null` and `symbol`. Everything else (plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, maps, class instances) is an **object**.

Primitives are immutable. `"abc".toUpperCase()` returns a new string; it never changes the original. When you call a method on a primitive, the engine temporarily wraps it in an object (`String`, `Number`...) so the method can run.

Variables hold primitives directly, but they hold objects by reference. Assigning or passing an object copies the reference, so two variables can point at the same object:

- `let a = 1; let b = a; b++` leaves `a` at 1.
- `const x = { n: 1 }; const y = x; y.n = 2` changes `x.n` too, because there is one object.

JavaScript is always pass-by-value. For objects the value being copied is the reference, which is why reassigning a parameter inside a function does not affect the caller, while mutating it does.

lesson.heading: typeof and its quirks
lesson.body:
`typeof` returns a string describing a value's type. Most results are what you expect, with two historical exceptions:

- `typeof null` is `"object"`. This is a bug from the first implementation that can never be fixed without breaking the web. Check for null with `value === null`.
- `typeof function () {}` is `"function"`, even though functions are objects.

Other useful facts: `typeof NaN` is `"number"`, `typeof []` is `"object"` (use `Array.isArray`), and `typeof undeclaredVariable` returns `"undefined"` instead of throwing (the one safe way to probe for an undeclared global).

code.source:
typeof "hi";        // "string"
typeof 42;          // "number"
typeof 10n;         // "bigint"
typeof Symbol();    // "symbol"
typeof undefined;   // "undefined"
typeof null;        // "object"  (legacy bug)
typeof [];          // "object"
typeof (() => {});  // "function"
Array.isArray([]);  // true

lesson.heading: Equality: ===, == and Object.is
lesson.body:
`===` (strict equality) compares without converting types. Two objects are strictly equal only if they are the same reference, so `{} === {}` is false.

`==` (loose equality) converts operands first, using a fixed algorithm:

- `null == undefined` is true, and neither equals anything else. So `null == 0` is false.
- If one side is a number and the other a string, the string is converted to a number: `"1" == 1` is true.
- Booleans are converted to numbers first: `true == "1"` is true, `true == "true"` is false.
- An object compared with a primitive is converted with `ToPrimitive` (`valueOf`, then `toString`): `[1] == 1` is true.

`Object.is` is like `===` except for two cases: `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true and `Object.is(0, -0)` is false. React uses `Object.is` to compare state and dependency values.

**Rule of thumb:** use `===` everywhere. The one common, readable exception is `value == null`, which checks for both `null` and `undefined` at once.

lesson.heading: Implicit coercion
lesson.body:
Operators convert operands to the types they need.

- **+** first converts both operands to primitives. If either result is a string, it concatenates. Otherwise it adds numbers. So `"5" + 2` is `"52"` but `"5" - 2` is `3`, because `-` only works on numbers.
- `[] + []` is `""` (both become empty strings). `[] + {}` is `"[object Object]"`.
- Relational operators (`<`, `>=`) convert to numbers. That is why `null >= 0` is true even though `null == 0` is false: `==` has the special null rule, `>=` does not.
- `Number("")` is 0, `Number(" 12 ")` is 12, `Number("12px")` is NaN, while `parseInt("12px", 10)` is 12 because it parses until the first invalid character.

Explicit conversion (`String(x)`, `Number(x)`, `Boolean(x)`) is clearer than relying on these rules.

code.source:
console.log("5" + 2);       // "52"
console.log("5" - 2);       // 3
console.log("5" * "2");     // 10
console.log(true + 1);      // 2
console.log([] + {});       // "[object Object]"
console.log(null == 0);     // false
console.log(null >= 0);     // true
console.log(parseInt("12px", 10)); // 12
console.log(Number("12px"));       // NaN

lesson.heading: Truthy, falsy, ?? and ?.
lesson.body:
In a boolean context every value is either truthy or falsy. The falsy values are: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]` and `{}`.

`||` returns the first truthy operand, which breaks defaults when 0 or "" are valid: `count || 10` turns a real 0 into 10. The nullish coalescing operator `??` only falls back on `null` or `undefined`: `count ?? 10` keeps 0.

Optional chaining `?.` stops and returns `undefined` if the left side is `null` or `undefined`: `user?.address?.city`, `fn?.()`, `arr?.[0]`.

lesson.heading: Numbers: floating point, NaN and BigInt
lesson.body:
Every `number` is an IEEE 754 64-bit float. Many decimals cannot be represented exactly, so `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Compare floats with a tolerance, or store money as integer cents.

Integers are exact only up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1). Beyond that, use `bigint` (`123n`). You cannot mix bigint and number in arithmetic without converting: `1n + 1` throws a TypeError.

`NaN` is the only value not equal to itself. Use `Number.isNaN(x)`, not the global `isNaN(x)`, which coerces first so `isNaN("hello")` is true.

code.source:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);                            // false
console.log(Math.abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON);   // true
console.log(Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2);                  // 9007199254740992 (wrong!)
console.log(9007199254740991n + 2n);                       // 9007199254740993n
console.log(NaN === NaN, Number.isNaN(NaN));               // false true
console.log(isNaN("hello"), Number.isNaN("hello"));        // true false

keyPoints: Seven primitives (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) plus objects.
Primitives are copied by value; objects are shared through references, but argument passing is still by value.
`typeof null` is "object"; check null with `=== null` and arrays with `Array.isArray`.
Prefer `===`; `x == null` is the accepted shortcut for null-or-undefined.
`+` concatenates if either operand becomes a string; other arithmetic operators convert to numbers.
Only 8 values are falsy; `[]`, `{}` and `"0"` are truthy.
Use `??` for defaults when 0 or empty string are valid values.
Floats are imprecise; use a tolerance, integer cents or bigint.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(typeof null);
questions.explanation: `typeof null` returns "object" because of a bug in the original implementation where null shared the object type tag. It was kept for web compatibility.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code: console.log([] + {});
questions.explanation: `+` converts both operands to primitives. `[]` becomes "" and `{}` becomes "[object Object]". One side is a string, so the result is string concatenation.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code: console.log("5" - "2" + "1");
questions.explanation: `-` forces numeric conversion: `"5" - "2"` is 3. Then `3 + "1"` has a string operand, so it concatenates to "31".

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code: console.log(null == 0, null >= 0);
questions.explanation: `==` has a special rule: null is only loosely equal to undefined, so `null == 0` is false. Relational operators like `>=` convert null to the number 0, so `null >= 0` is true.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code:
const qty = 0;
console.log(qty || 10, qty ?? 10);
questions.explanation: `||` falls back on any falsy value, and 0 is falsy, so the first gives 10. `??` only falls back on null or undefined, so the second keeps 0.

questions.prompt: Which check correctly detects NaN without false positives?
questions.explanation: NaN is never equal to anything, including itself, so the equality checks are always false. Global `isNaN` coerces its argument first, so `isNaN("abc")` is true. `Number.isNaN` returns true only for the actual NaN value (`Object.is(x, NaN)` also works).

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code: console.log({ a: 1 } === { a: 1 });
questions.explanation: The two literals create two different objects. Strict equality on objects compares references, not contents.

questions.prompt: `typeof NaN` returns "number".
questions.explanation: NaN (Not-a-Number) is a special value of the number type defined by IEEE 754, so typeof reports "number".

questions.prompt: `Object.is(0, -0)` returns true, just like `0 === -0`.
questions.explanation: `0 === -0` is true, but `Object.is` distinguishes signed zeros and returns false. It also treats NaN as equal to NaN.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which values are falsy?
questions.explanation: The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN. The string "0" is non-empty, and every object (including empty arrays and objects) is truthy.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the operator ___ returns its right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined.
questions.explanation: `??` is the nullish coalescing operator. Unlike `||`, it does not treat 0, "" or false as missing.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between == and ===, and when (if ever) would you use ==?
questions.answer:
- `===` compares type and value with no conversion; objects are equal only if they are the same reference.
- `==` runs the Abstract Equality algorithm: null and undefined equal each other and nothing else, strings and booleans are converted to numbers, objects are converted with ToPrimitive. This gives results like `[1] == 1` and `"" == 0` being true.
- I default to `===` (and enforce it with ESLint `eqeqeq`) because it is predictable.
- The one idiom I accept is `value == null` to check for null or undefined in one comparison; many style guides allow it explicitly.
- For NaN and signed zero edge cases I use `Object.is` or `Number.isNaN`.

questions.prompt: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not equal to 0.3 in JavaScript, and how do you handle money?
questions.answer:
- All JS numbers are IEEE 754 double-precision floats. 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so their stored values are tiny approximations and the sum is 0.30000000000000004.
- This is not JS-specific; Python, Java doubles and C behave the same.
- To compare floats, check that the difference is under a tolerance such as `Number.EPSILON` scaled to the magnitude.
- For money I store integer minor units (cents) or use `bigint`, and format only at the edges with `Intl.NumberFormat`. For complex decimal math a decimal library is safer.
- I also keep in mind that integers are only exact up to 2^53 - 1, which matters for IDs from 64-bit databases; those should travel as strings or bigint.

questions.prompt: Explain how primitives and objects differ when passed to a function. Is JavaScript pass-by-reference?
questions.answer:
- JavaScript is always pass-by-value. For primitives the value is the data itself; for objects the value is a reference to the object.
- So a function that mutates a parameter object (`obj.x = 1`) changes what the caller sees, because both hold references to the same object.
- But reassigning the parameter (`obj = {}`) only rebinds the local variable; the caller still points at the original. True pass-by-reference (like C++ `&`) would change the caller's variable.
- In practice this is why React and Redux insist on immutable updates: if you mutate shared objects, reference equality checks cannot detect the change.

questions.prompt: Walk me through how JavaScript evaluates [] == ![].
questions.answer:
- `![]` runs first. Arrays are truthy, so `![]` is `false`. The comparison is now `[] == false`.
- With `==`, a boolean operand is converted to a number: `false` becomes `0`, giving `[] == 0`.
- An object compared with a number goes through ToPrimitive: `[].valueOf()` returns the array itself (not primitive), so `toString()` is used and returns `""`. Now `"" == 0`.
- A string compared with a number is converted to a number: `Number("")` is 0, so `0 == 0` is true.
- The takeaway I would give in an interview: knowing the algorithm explains the puzzle, but the fix in real code is to use `===` and explicit conversions.

chapters.title: Scope, Hoisting and the TDZ
chapters.summary: How var, let and const are scoped, what hoisting really does, and why the temporal dead zone exists.

lesson.heading: Kinds of scope
lesson.body:
Scope decides where a name is visible. JavaScript has:

- **Global scope**: names declared at the top of a classic script.
- **Module scope**: each ES module has its own top-level scope; nothing leaks to `globalThis` unless you assign it explicitly.
- **Function scope**: created by every function call.
- **Block scope**: created by `{ }` blocks (if, for, while, bare blocks) for `let`, `const` and `class`.

Scope is **lexical** (static): it depends on where code is written, not where it is called from. When a name is looked up, the engine checks the current scope, then the enclosing scope, and so on up to global. This is the **scope chain**. If the name is never found you get a ReferenceError.

lesson.heading: var, let and const
lesson.body:
- `var` is function-scoped (it ignores blocks), can be redeclared, and at the top level of a classic script it creates a property on `window`.
- `let` is block-scoped, cannot be redeclared in the same scope, and can be reassigned.
- `const` is block-scoped and cannot be reassigned. It must be initialized at declaration.

`const` makes the **binding** constant, not the value. `const user = {}; user.name = "A"` is fine. Use `Object.freeze` for a shallow read-only object.

Modern style: use `const` by default, `let` when you need to reassign, and avoid `var`.

lesson.heading: Hoisting
lesson.body:
Before running a scope, the engine processes its declarations. This is called hoisting. Nothing physically moves; the names are registered when the scope is created.

- **Function declarations** are hoisted with their body, so you can call them before the line they appear on.
- **var** declarations are hoisted and initialized to `undefined`. Reading one early gives `undefined`, not an error. The assignment stays where it is.
- **let, const and class** are hoisted too (the scope knows about them), but they are left **uninitialized** until their declaration line runs.
- **Function expressions** and arrow functions follow the rule of the variable that holds them. `var f = function () {}` gives `f` = undefined early, so calling it throws "f is not a function".

lesson.heading: The temporal dead zone
lesson.body:
The **temporal dead zone (TDZ)** is the time between entering a scope and the evaluation of a `let`, `const` or `class` declaration. Touching the name in that window throws a ReferenceError ("Cannot access 'x' before initialization").

It is "temporal" because it is about time of execution, not position in the text. A function defined above the declaration can safely use the variable as long as it is **called** after the declaration runs.

The TDZ also explains shadowing surprises: an inner `let x` shadows an outer `x` for the whole block, including lines before its declaration. Even `typeof x` throws inside the TDZ.

Why it exists: it catches use-before-initialization bugs, and it gives `const` sane semantics (a const should never be observed with a value other than the one it was declared with).

lesson.heading: The classic loop and closure bug
lesson.body:
Callbacks created in a loop capture variables, not values. With `var` there is one `i` for the whole function, so every callback sees its final value. With `let`, the spec creates a fresh binding for each iteration, so each callback captures its own `i`.

Before `let` existed, the fix was an IIFE that copied `i` into a new function scope. You will still see this in older code and interview questions.

keyPoints: Scope is lexical: it is decided by where code is written.
`var` is function-scoped; `let` and `const` are block-scoped.
`const` prevents reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the object.
Function declarations are fully hoisted; `var` is hoisted as undefined.
`let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted but uninitialized: the TDZ.
An inner `let` shadows the outer name for the entire block, even before its line.
`let` in a for loop creates a new binding per iteration, fixing the classic setTimeout bug.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.code:
console.log(a);
var a = 1;
questions.explanation: The `var a` declaration is hoisted and initialized to undefined. The assignment `a = 1` happens on its own line, after the log.

questions.prompt: What happens here?
questions.code:
console.log(b);
let b = 1;
questions.explanation: `let b` is hoisted but uninitialized. Reading it before the declaration runs is a TDZ access and throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization`.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: `var i` is a single function-scoped binding. The callbacks run after the loop finishes, when i is 3, and all three read the same variable.

questions.prompt: What is logged?
options: TypeError: run is not a function
questions.explanation: `var run` is hoisted as undefined; the function expression is only assigned later. Calling undefined throws a TypeError.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: The inner `let x` shadows the outer x for the whole block. At the log line the inner x is in its temporal dead zone, so it throws instead of falling back to the outer x.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: `const` only stops reassignment of the binding. Mutating a property of the object it points to is allowed.

questions.prompt: In a classic (non-module) browser script, what does this log?
questions.explanation: Top-level `var` in a classic script creates a property on the global object (`window`). Top-level `let` and `const` live in a separate declarative scope and do not become window properties.

questions.prompt: `let` and `const` declarations are not hoisted at all.
questions.explanation: They are hoisted in the sense that the scope registers them at creation, which is exactly why an inner `let` shadows an outer variable before its line. They are just not initialized, so access throws (the TDZ).

questions.prompt: A function can reference a `const` declared below it, as long as the function is called after the const line has executed.
questions.explanation: The TDZ is about execution time, not source position. By the time the function runs, the const is initialized.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which can be used before their declaration line executes without throwing?
options: A var variable (reading it gives undefined)
An arrow function stored in a const
questions.explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their body and var is hoisted as undefined. let, const and class bindings are in the TDZ until their declaration runs, so the arrow in a const is unusable too.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the window between entering a scope and evaluating a let or const declaration is called the ___.
questions.explanation: Accessing the binding during the temporal dead zone throws a ReferenceError.

questions.prompt: What is hoisting? Explain how it differs for var, let/const, function declarations and function expressions.
questions.answer:
- Hoisting is the effect of the engine creating all bindings for a scope before executing its code.
- Function declarations are created and initialized with their body, so they are callable anywhere in the scope.
- `var` bindings are created and initialized to `undefined`; the assignment stays in place, so early reads return undefined.
- `let`, `const` and `class` bindings are created but not initialized. Accessing them before the declaration executes throws a ReferenceError (the TDZ).
- Function expressions and arrows behave like whatever variable holds them: with var you get "is not a function", with const you get a TDZ ReferenceError.
- I'd mention that nothing is literally moved to the top; the "move to top" picture is a mental model.

questions.prompt: Compare var, let and const. Which do you use and why?
questions.answer:
- Scope: var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped.
- Redeclaration: var allows it silently; let and const throw a SyntaxError in the same scope.
- Hoisting: var is initialized to undefined; let and const sit in the TDZ.
- Globals: top-level var in a classic script creates a `window` property; let and const do not.
- Loops: let gets a fresh binding per iteration, which fixes closure-in-loop bugs.
- I use const by default because it signals the binding never changes, let when I must reassign (counters, accumulators), and never var in new code. I also point out that const does not make objects immutable.

questions.prompt: Why does the language have a temporal dead zone instead of just initializing let to undefined like var?
questions.answer:
- Reading a variable before it is initialized is almost always a bug; the TDZ turns that silent `undefined` into a loud error at the faulty line.
- It is needed for `const` to make sense: a const must never be observed with any value other than its initializer, so it cannot be undefined first.
- It keeps shadowing honest: inside a block that declares `let x`, every reference to x means the inner one, so you cannot accidentally read the outer x on early lines.
- Classes use it too, so `new Foo()` before `class Foo` fails clearly instead of producing a half-defined object.

questions.prompt: Here is a loop that schedules three setTimeout calls with var and prints 3 3 3. Give two ways to fix it and explain why they work.
questions.answer:
- Cause: var creates one function-scoped `i`. The callbacks close over that single binding and run after the loop ends, when i is 3.
- Fix 1: use `let`. The for-loop spec copies the binding into a new lexical environment for each iteration, so each callback closes over its own i.
- Fix 2 (older code): wrap the body in an IIFE `(function (j) { setTimeout(() => log(j)); })(i)`, which creates a new function scope per iteration holding a copy of the value.
- Fix 3: pass the value as an argument: `setTimeout(console.log, 0, i)` or `setTimeout(log.bind(null, i))`, which captures the value at scheduling time.

chapters.title: Functions and Closures
chapters.summary: Function forms, arrow function differences, higher-order functions and closures with real use cases and pitfalls.

lesson.heading: Function forms
lesson.body:
Functions are first-class values: you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments and return them.

- **Declaration**: `function add(a, b) { }`. Hoisted with its body.
- **Expression**: `const add = function (a, b) { }`. Can be named for better stack traces.
- **Arrow**: `const add = (a, b) => a + b`. Concise, with different `this` rules.
- **Method shorthand**: `{ add(a, b) { } }` inside objects and classes.

Parameters support defaults and rest syntax. Default values are evaluated **at call time**, every time, and can refer to earlier parameters.

lesson.heading: Arrow functions are different
lesson.body:
Arrow functions are not just shorter syntax. Compared with regular functions they:

- have no own `this`; they use `this` from the enclosing scope (lexical this)
- have no own `arguments` object (use rest parameters instead)
- cannot be called with `new` and have no `prototype` property
- cannot be generators

That makes arrows ideal for callbacks inside methods (they keep the method's `this`) and a bad choice for object methods that need `this` to be the object.

Returning an object literal from a concise arrow needs parentheses: `() => ({ ok: true })`. Without them the braces are read as a function body.

lesson.heading: Higher-order functions
lesson.body:
A higher-order function takes a function as an argument or returns one. `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `addEventListener` and `setTimeout` are all examples.

Returning functions is how you build function factories, partial application and decorators that wrap behavior (logging, caching, retry). These patterns rely on closures.

lesson.heading: What a closure is
lesson.body:
A **closure** is a function together with a reference to the scope it was created in. Because scope is lexical, a function can always read and write the variables that were visible where it was defined, even after the outer function has returned.

The important word is **reference**: a closure does not copy values. If the captured variable changes later, the closure sees the new value. Each call of the outer function creates a new scope, so each returned closure gets its own private state.

lesson.heading: Practical closures: once and memoize
lesson.body:
Closures are everywhere in real code:

- **Encapsulation**: private state without classes (the counter above, the old module pattern).
- **Function factories** and partial application.
- **Callbacks** that remember context (event handlers, React hooks).
- **Caching**: memoize stores results in a closed-over `Map`.
- **Run-once logic**: `once` remembers whether it already ran.

Pitfalls: a closure keeps its whole captured scope alive, which can retain large objects in memory, and it can read **stale** values if it was created during an earlier render or iteration (the classic React stale-closure bug with `useEffect` and intervals).

keyPoints: Functions are first-class values; higher-order functions take or return functions.
Default parameters are evaluated on every call and can reference earlier parameters.
Arrows have lexical `this`, no `arguments`, no `prototype` and cannot be used with `new`.
A closure is a function plus a live reference to the scope it was defined in.
Closures capture variables, not snapshots of values.
Each call of an outer function creates fresh, independent closed-over state.
Closures power memoization, once, factories, private state and event handlers, but can retain memory and read stale values.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: The returned arrow closes over the same `count` variable. Each call increments the shared closed-over value.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: Each call to `counter()` creates a new scope with its own count. `a` was called twice, `b` once.

questions.prompt: What does f(3) return?
questions.explanation: Default parameters are evaluated at call time and can use earlier parameters. b defaults to 3 * 2 = 6, so the result is 3 + 6.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: Closures hold a reference to the variable, not a copy of its value at creation time. By the time `show` runs, `x` has been reassigned to 20.

questions.prompt: What does this return?
questions.code:
const make = () => { ok: true };
make();
questions.explanation: Without parentheses the braces are a function body, and `ok:` is parsed as a label followed by the expression `true`. The body has no return statement, so the result is undefined. Write `() => ({ ok: true })`.

questions.prompt: This runs at the top level of an ES module. What happens?
questions.code:
const f = () => arguments;
console.log(f(1, 2));
options: Throws ReferenceError: arguments is not defined
questions.explanation: Arrow functions have no own `arguments`, so the name is looked up in the enclosing scope. Module top level has no `arguments` binding, so it throws. Inside a regular function the arrow would see that outer function's arguments instead. Use rest parameters `(...args) =>`.

questions.prompt: A closure copies the values of outer variables at the moment the inner function is created.
questions.explanation: A closure keeps a reference to the outer scope (environment record). Later changes to those variables are visible to the closure.

questions.prompt: Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors with `new`.
questions.explanation: Arrows have no [[Construct]] internal method and no prototype property, so `new` throws a TypeError.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are true about arrow functions?
options: They inherit `this` from the enclosing scope
questions.explanation: Arrows use lexical this, which call/apply/bind cannot override (only the arguments are passed). They lack an own arguments object, cannot be generators and have no prototype.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a function bundled with a reference to the lexical scope where it was defined is called a ___.
questions.explanation: That combination is a closure. Every JavaScript function forms one, but it only becomes interesting when the function outlives the scope it came from.

questions.prompt: What is a closure? Give two real-world uses.
questions.answer:
- A closure is a function combined with a reference to the lexical environment it was created in, so it can keep accessing those variables after the outer function returns.
- Use 1: encapsulation. A factory like `createStore()` keeps state in a local variable and exposes only functions that read and update it, so nothing outside can mutate it directly.
- Use 2: caching or rate limiting. `memoize`, `once`, `debounce` and `throttle` all keep their cache, flag or timer id in a closure.
- Others: event handlers that remember an item id, partial application, React hooks (every render's handlers close over that render's props and state).
- Trade-offs: captured scopes stay alive as long as the closure does, so long-lived closures can retain memory; and closures read whatever the variable holds when they run, which can be stale.

questions.prompt: Implement a memoize function. What are its limitations?
questions.answer:
- Basic version: `function memoize(fn) { const cache = new Map(); return function (...args) { const key = JSON.stringify(args); if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key); const r = fn.apply(this, args); cache.set(key, r); return r; }; }`
- The cache lives in a closure, so each memoized function has its own.
- Limitations: JSON keys fail for functions, cycles and distinguish `{a,b}` order; object arguments with the same contents collide or differ unexpectedly. For single object arguments a `WeakMap` keyed by reference avoids leaks.
- The cache grows forever unless bounded (LRU, TTL).
- Only safe for pure functions; side effects or time-dependent results break it.
- For async functions, cache the promise so concurrent calls share one request, and evict on rejection.

questions.prompt: Explain the stale closure problem, for example in a React interval.
questions.answer:
- A closure reads the variables of the scope it was created in. In React, each render is a new function call with its own props and state, so each render's callbacks close over that render's values.
- If `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])` runs only once, the interval callback captures `count` from the first render (0) forever, so the count goes to 1 and stays.
- Fixes: use the functional updater `setCount(c => c + 1)` so the callback does not read count; include count in the dependency array so the effect re-subscribes; or keep the latest value in a ref.
- The general lesson: long-lived callbacks need a way to read current values, not values captured at creation.

questions.prompt: When would you not use an arrow function?
questions.answer:
- Object methods that use `this`: `{ name: "a", hi: () => this.name }` reads the outer this, not the object.
- Prototype or class methods meant to be shared: a class field arrow creates a new function per instance (more memory) and cannot be overridden through `super` cleanly.
- Constructors: arrows cannot be called with new.
- DOM event handlers where you want `this` to be the element (though `event.currentTarget` works with arrows).
- Functions that need `arguments`, or generators.
- Arrows are my default for callbacks and small utilities, especially inside methods where lexical this is exactly what I want.

chapters.title: this, call, apply and bind
chapters.summary: How this is decided at call time, the four binding rules and their precedence, and how to stop losing this.

lesson.heading: this is decided by the call, not the definition
lesson.body:
For regular functions, `this` is not fixed when the function is written. It is set every time the function is **called**, based on how it is called. The same function can see different `this` values on different calls.

Arrow functions are the exception: they have no `this` of their own and use the `this` of the scope they were defined in.

To figure out `this` for a regular function call, look at the call site and apply the rules below in order of precedence.

lesson.heading: The four binding rules
lesson.body:
From highest to lowest precedence:

- **new binding**: `new Foo()` creates a fresh object, sets its prototype to `Foo.prototype` and uses it as `this`.
- **Explicit binding**: `fn.call(obj)`, `fn.apply(obj)` or a function produced by `fn.bind(obj)` use `obj`.
- **Implicit binding**: `obj.method()` uses the object before the dot. Only the last object in the chain counts: in `a.b.c()`, `this` is `a.b`.
- **Default binding**: a plain call `fn()` gets `undefined` in strict mode (which includes ES modules and class bodies) and `globalThis` in sloppy mode.

`new` beats `bind`: calling `new` on a bound function ignores the bound `this` (bound arguments are still applied).

lesson.heading: Losing this
lesson.body:
The most common bug: a method is taken off its object and called as a plain function. The call site no longer has an object before the dot, so the default rule applies.

This happens when you:

- assign a method to a variable: `const f = obj.method; f()`
- pass a method as a callback: `setTimeout(obj.method, 100)`, `button.addEventListener("click", obj.method)`, `arr.map(obj.method)`
- destructure it: `const { method } = obj`

Fixes: bind it (`obj.method.bind(obj)`), wrap it in an arrow (`() => obj.method()`), or define it as an arrow class field so it captures the instance. Many array methods also take a `thisArg` (`arr.map(fn, obj)`).

lesson.heading: Arrow functions and lexical this
lesson.body:
An arrow function looks up `this` like any other variable: in its enclosing scope. `call`, `apply` and `bind` cannot change it.

This is exactly what you want for callbacks inside methods, and exactly wrong for methods on object literals. An arrow defined directly in an object literal does not see the object, because object literals do not create a scope; it sees the `this` of the surrounding code (`undefined` in a module).

lesson.heading: call, apply and bind
lesson.body:
- `fn.call(thisArg, a, b)` calls immediately with arguments listed individually.
- `fn.apply(thisArg, [a, b])` calls immediately with arguments as an array (handy before spread existed: `Math.max.apply(null, nums)`).
- `fn.bind(thisArg, a)` does not call. It returns a new function with `this` permanently set and optional leading arguments pre-filled (partial application).

A bound function cannot be re-bound: `f.bind(a).bind(b)` still uses `a`. Only `new` can override it.

A simplified `bind` polyfill shows how it works with closures:

keyPoints: For regular functions, `this` depends on how the function is called.
Precedence: new > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (obj.method()) > default.
Default binding is `undefined` in strict mode, modules and classes; `globalThis` in sloppy scripts.
Extracting or passing a method as a callback loses its `this`.
Arrow functions take `this` lexically and ignore call/apply/bind.
`bind` returns a new function; it cannot be re-bound, but `new` overrides its this.
`call` takes arguments individually, `apply` takes an array.

questions.prompt: This code is in an ES module. What does it log?
questions.explanation: `user.hi()` uses implicit binding, so this is user. `hi()` is a plain call; modules are strict, so this is undefined and `this?.name` is undefined.

questions.prompt: This code is in an ES module. What does it log?
questions.code:
const obj = { whoami: () => this };
console.log(obj.whoami());
questions.explanation: Object literals do not create a scope for `this`. The arrow takes this from the module top level, which is undefined.

questions.prompt: What does g() return?
questions.explanation: The first bind fixes this to `{ x: 1 }`. Binding a bound function again creates a wrapper, but the inner call still uses the original bound this.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: new binding has higher precedence than bind. The bound this is ignored and the newly created object is used, so name is "new".

questions.prompt: What does this log?
questions.explanation: Class bodies are always strict mode. `f()` is a plain call, so this is undefined, and reading `undefined.n` throws a TypeError.

questions.prompt: This code is in an ES module. What do the two calls return?
questions.explanation: The regular function callback is called by map with no thisArg, so default binding gives undefined. The arrow inherits this from `viaArrow`, which was called as `obj.viaArrow()`.

questions.prompt: What does this return?
questions.code: Math.max.apply(null, [1, 5, 3]);
questions.explanation: `apply` spreads the array as individual arguments, so this is `Math.max(1, 5, 3)`. Today you would write `Math.max(...nums)`.

questions.prompt: For a regular function, `this` is determined where the function is defined.
questions.explanation: That describes arrow functions. Regular functions get this from the call site each time they are called.

questions.prompt: `fn.bind(obj)` calls `fn` immediately with this set to obj.
questions.explanation: bind returns a new function and does not call anything. `call` and `apply` invoke immediately.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which calls run `fn` with this set to `obj` (fn is a regular function)?
options: `const o = { fn }; const g = o.fn; g()`
questions.explanation: call, apply and bind set this explicitly, and many array methods accept a thisArg. The last one extracts the method and calls it plainly, so default binding applies.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `fn.___(obj)` returns a new function whose this is permanently obj.
questions.explanation: `bind` creates a bound function. Only `new` can override its this.

questions.prompt: Explain how this is determined in JavaScript, including precedence.
questions.answer:
- For arrow functions, this is lexical: it comes from the enclosing scope and nothing at the call site changes it.
- For regular functions, it is decided per call: new binding (fresh object) beats explicit binding (call, apply, bind), which beats implicit binding (the object before the dot), which beats default binding.
- Default binding is undefined in strict code (modules, classes, "use strict") and globalThis in sloppy scripts.
- Edge cases: bound functions ignore later call/apply/bind but not new; callbacks lose implicit binding; DOM listeners registered with a regular function get the element (`currentTarget`) as this.
- I usually explain it by pointing at the call site: "what is to the left of the dot when this runs?"

questions.prompt: Implement Function.prototype.bind without using bind.
questions.answer:
- Store the original function: `const fn = this`.
- Return a new function that merges preset and call-time arguments and calls `fn.apply(ctx, [...preset, ...args])`.
- Handle `new`: if the bound function is called with new (`new.target` is set), construct with the original function instead of applying ctx, so `new` wins as the spec requires.
- Preserve the prototype chain so `instanceof` works (the spec's bound functions do this via the target's prototype; a polyfill sets `bound.prototype = Object.create(fn.prototype)`).
- Optionally throw a TypeError if `this` is not callable.
- I'd mention that real bound functions also have a `name` of "bound fn" and a `length` reduced by the preset count.

questions.prompt: Why did React class components need this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)?
questions.answer:
- In JSX, `onClick={this.handleClick}` passes the method as a callback. React later calls it as a plain function, so implicit binding is lost.
- Class bodies are strict mode, so this inside the handler is undefined and `this.setState` throws.
- Binding in the constructor creates one bound function per instance that always has the component as this.
- Alternatives: class field arrows (`handleClick = () => {}`) capture the instance lexically; inline arrows in render (`onClick={() => this.handleClick()}`) work but create a new function each render.
- Function components with hooks avoid the issue because they do not use this at all.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between call, apply and bind? Give a use case for each.
questions.answer:
- `call(thisArg, ...args)` invokes now with listed arguments. Use case: borrowing a method, e.g. `Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)` or calling a parent constructor in pre-class code: `Parent.call(this, name)`.
- `apply(thisArg, argsArray)` invokes now with an array of arguments. Use case: forwarding all arguments in a wrapper, `fn.apply(this, args)`, or `Math.max.apply(null, nums)` (now usually spread).
- `bind(thisArg, ...preset)` returns a new function for later. Use case: passing a method as an event handler or timer callback, or partial application like `const log = console.log.bind(console, "[app]")`.
- Note that none of them affect arrow functions' this.

chapters.title: Prototypes and Classes
chapters.summary: The prototype chain, what new does, and how class syntax, private fields and inheritance map onto prototypes.

lesson.heading: The prototype chain
lesson.body:
Every object has an internal link, `[[Prototype]]`, to another object or `null`. When you read a property that the object does not have, the engine follows that link and looks there, and so on up the chain until it reaches `null`. This is **prototypal inheritance**: objects delegate to other objects.

- Read it with `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`; the legacy accessor `obj.__proto__` does the same.
- **Writes** do not walk the chain. Assigning `obj.x = 1` creates or updates an own property on `obj`, which shadows any `x` further up.
- `Object.hasOwn(obj, "x")` checks only own properties; the `in` operator checks the whole chain.

Arrays get their methods this way: `[].map` is found on `Array.prototype`, whose prototype is `Object.prototype`, whose prototype is `null`.

code.source:
const animal = { eats: true, describe() { return "eats: " + this.eats; } };
const rabbit = Object.create(animal);   // rabbit -> animal -> Object.prototype -> null
rabbit.jumps = true;

rabbit.eats;                 // true (found on animal)
rabbit.describe();           // "eats: true" (this is rabbit)
Object.hasOwn(rabbit, "eats"); // false
"eats" in rabbit;            // true

rabbit.eats = false;         // creates an own property, animal is unchanged
animal.eats;                 // true

lesson.heading: prototype vs __proto__ and what new does
lesson.body:
These two names cause most of the confusion:

- `Foo.prototype` is an ordinary property that exists on functions. It is the object that will become the prototype of instances created with `new Foo()`.
- `obj.__proto__` (or `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`) is the actual prototype link of an object.

So `new Foo().__proto__ === Foo.prototype`.

`new Foo(args)` does four things:

- creates an empty object
- links its prototype to `Foo.prototype`
- calls `Foo` with `this` bound to the new object
- returns the new object, unless `Foo` explicitly returns another object

`instanceof` checks whether `Foo.prototype` appears anywhere in the object's prototype chain. Replacing `Foo.prototype` after creating instances therefore makes `instanceof` return false for them.

lesson.heading: Classes are prototypes with better syntax
lesson.body:
`class` does not add a new object model. Methods go on `Class.prototype`, and instances delegate to it just like with constructor functions. What class syntax adds:

- class bodies are always strict mode
- methods are non-enumerable (they do not show up in `for...in`)
- calling a class without `new` throws a TypeError
- class declarations are in the TDZ until evaluated (not usable before the line)
- `static` members live on the constructor itself
- **class fields** (`count = 0`) are own properties created on each instance during construction
- **private elements** (`#secret`, `#helper()`) are truly inaccessible outside the class body; `#x in obj` checks for them
- `static { }` blocks for one-time setup

lesson.heading: Inheritance with extends and super
lesson.body:
`class B extends A` sets up two prototype links: `B.prototype` delegates to `A.prototype` (instance methods) and `B` delegates to `A` (static methods).

In a derived class constructor you **must** call `super(...)` before touching `this`, because the parent constructor is what creates the object. Using `this` first throws a ReferenceError. If you omit the constructor entirely, a default one that forwards all arguments to `super` is generated.

`super.method()` calls the parent's version of a method, which is how you extend rather than replace behavior.

lesson.heading: Gotchas and design advice
lesson.body:
- **Shared mutable state on the prototype**: putting an array or object on the prototype means every instance shares it. Initialize per-instance data in the constructor or with class fields.
- **Arrow class fields** bind `this` but create one function per instance and are not on the prototype, so subclasses cannot call them with `super`.
- `Object.create(null)` makes an object with no prototype: useful as a pure dictionary since keys like `"toString"` or `"__proto__"` cannot collide with inherited ones (though `Map` is usually better).
- Deep inheritance hierarchies get brittle. Prefer composition (objects that hold other objects or functions) when you only need to share behavior.

keyPoints: Property reads walk the prototype chain; writes create own properties that shadow.
`Foo.prototype` becomes the prototype of objects created by `new Foo()`.
`new` creates an object, links its prototype, runs the constructor with that this, and returns it.
`instanceof` searches the prototype chain for `Foo.prototype`.
Classes use prototypes underneath, but are strict, require `new`, and have non-enumerable methods.
Call `super()` before using `this` in a derived constructor.
`#private` fields are enforced by the language; class fields are per-instance own properties.
Never put mutable shared data on a prototype by accident.

questions.explanation: `tricks` lives on `Dog.prototype`, so both instances read the same array. `a.tricks.push` mutates that shared array; it does not create an own property.

questions.prompt: What does this log?

const o = Object.create(null);
console.log(typeof o.toString);
questions.explanation: `Object.create(null)` creates an object whose prototype is null, so nothing (including toString) is inherited from Object.prototype.

questions.prompt: What does this log?
options: TypeError: Class constructor Dog cannot be invoked without 'new'
questions.explanation: Unlike constructor functions, classes throw if called without new. This prevents the old bug where forgetting new wrote properties onto the global object.

questions.prompt: What does this log?

questions.prompt: ES2015 classes introduced a new, separate object model that replaces prototypes.
questions.explanation: Classes are mostly syntax over the same prototype mechanism. `typeof SomeClass` is "function" and its methods live on `SomeClass.prototype`.

questions.prompt: Methods defined in a class body are non-enumerable.
questions.explanation: Class methods are defined with enumerable: false, unlike methods assigned to `Foo.prototype.method = ...` in constructor-function code.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: what does `new Foo()` do?
options: Sets the new object's prototype to `Foo.prototype`
Copies all methods from `Foo.prototype` onto the object
Calls Foo with this bound to the new object
Returns the new object unless Foo returns another object
questions.explanation: Methods are not copied. Instances delegate to the prototype at lookup time, which is why adding a method to the prototype later makes it available to existing instances.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: `Object.___(proto)` creates a new object whose prototype is proto.
questions.explanation: `Object.create(proto)` links a new object to proto without running any constructor. `Object.create(null)` makes a prototype-less object.

questions.prompt: Explain prototypal inheritance and how it differs from classical inheritance.
questions.answer:
- In JavaScript, objects link to other objects. A property lookup that misses on the object follows the [[Prototype]] link up the chain until it finds the property or hits null.
- Behavior is shared by delegation at lookup time, not by copying. Changing a prototype immediately affects all objects that delegate to it.
- In classical languages (Java, C#), classes are blueprints and instances are created from them with a fixed shape; inheritance is between classes at compile time.
- JS class syntax looks classical but compiles to prototypes: methods on `Class.prototype`, `extends` linking prototypes and constructors.
- Practical consequences: you can create objects from other objects (`Object.create`), patch prototypes at runtime (which is how polyfills work), and writes shadow rather than modify inherited properties.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between __proto__ and prototype?
questions.answer:
- `prototype` is a regular property on functions (and classes). It holds the object that instances created with `new` will delegate to.
- `__proto__` is a legacy accessor on Object.prototype that exposes an object's actual [[Prototype]] link. Modern code uses `Object.getPrototypeOf` and `Object.setPrototypeOf` (or `Object.create`).
- The connection: `new Foo().__proto__ === Foo.prototype`.
- Plain objects do not have a `prototype` property; only functions do (and arrow functions and methods do not, since they cannot be constructors).
- I would avoid `setPrototypeOf` on hot objects, because changing an object's prototype after creation deoptimizes it in engines.

questions.prompt: How do private class fields (#x) compare to closures or naming conventions like _x for privacy?
questions.answer:
- `_x` is only a convention; anyone can read and write it.
- Closures give real privacy (the variable is not reachable), but methods must be created per instance inside the constructor, so they are not shared on the prototype.
- `#x` fields are enforced by the language: accessing them outside the class body is a SyntaxError, they do not show in `Object.keys` or JSON, and methods stay on the prototype.
- `#x in obj` gives a reliable brand check, better than instanceof which can be fooled across realms or by prototype changes.
- Limitations: subclasses cannot access a parent's private fields, and Proxies wrapping an instance break private access because the proxy is not the original object.

questions.prompt: When would you choose composition over inheritance in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
- Inheritance fits a true "is-a" relationship with a stable base, such as custom Error subclasses or framework base classes.
- Composition fits when objects need to share pieces of behavior across unrelated types: give an object functions or collaborators (a logger, a storage adapter) instead of extending a class that has them.
- Deep hierarchies cause the fragile base class problem: changing the parent breaks children in unexpected ways, and you end up inheriting methods you do not want.
- In JS composition is cheap: factory functions returning objects, mixing in functions with object spread, or dependency injection via constructor parameters.
- Modern frontend code reflects this: React moved from class inheritance to hooks, which compose behavior through functions.

chapters.title: DOM, Events and Delegation
chapters.summary: Querying and updating the DOM efficiently, the three phases of event propagation, and event delegation.

lesson.heading: Querying and updating the DOM
lesson.body:
The DOM is a tree of node objects that the browser builds from HTML. JavaScript reads and changes it through the `document` API.

- `querySelector` returns the first match or null; `querySelectorAll` returns a **static** NodeList (a snapshot).
- `getElementsByClassName` and `getElementsByTagName` return a **live** HTMLCollection that updates as the DOM changes.
- `element.closest(selector)` walks up from an element to the nearest matching ancestor (including itself).

Writing content:

- `textContent` sets plain text and is safe for user data.
- `innerHTML` parses HTML. Never put untrusted strings into it; that is a classic XSS hole.
- `innerText` is layout-aware (respects CSS visibility) and therefore slower because it can force layout.

To add many nodes, build them in a `DocumentFragment` or use `append(...nodes)` so the live DOM is touched once.

lesson.heading: Avoiding layout thrashing
lesson.body:
Reading layout properties (`offsetHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `scrollTop`, `getComputedStyle`) forces the browser to compute layout if there are pending style changes. If you alternate writes and reads in a loop, each read forces a synchronous layout. This is **layout thrashing** (forced synchronous layout).

Fix it by batching: do all reads first, then all writes, or schedule writes with `requestAnimationFrame`. Animate `transform` and `opacity` instead of `top` or `width` where possible, since they can skip layout.

lesson.heading: Event propagation: capture, target, bubble
lesson.body:
When an event fires on an element, it travels in three phases:

- **Capture**: from `window` down through ancestors to the target's parent.
- **Target**: at the element where the event happened.
- **Bubble**: back up from the target to `window`.

`addEventListener(type, fn)` listens in the bubble phase by default. Pass `{ capture: true }` (or `true`) to listen during capture.

Inside a listener:

- `event.target` is the element where the event originated (for a click, the innermost element clicked).
- `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running now.
- `event.stopPropagation()` stops the event moving to other elements; other listeners on the current element still run.
- `event.stopImmediatePropagation()` also stops the remaining listeners on the current element.
- `event.preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form). It does not stop propagation.

Some events do not bubble: `focus`, `blur`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`. Use `focusin`/`focusout` or `mouseover`/`mouseout` when you need bubbling versions.

lesson.heading: Event delegation
lesson.body:
Instead of attaching a listener to every child, attach one to a common ancestor and use `event.target` to work out which child was involved. This works because most events bubble.

Benefits:

- one listener instead of hundreds, so less memory and setup time
- elements added later are handled automatically
- no need to remove listeners when children are removed

Use `event.target.closest(selector)` because the click may land on a nested element (an icon inside a button). Check that the match is inside the container you delegated from.

lesson.heading: Listener options and cleanup
lesson.body:
`addEventListener` accepts an options object:

- `once: true` removes the listener after the first call.
- `passive: true` promises you will not call `preventDefault`. Browsers can then scroll without waiting for your handler. Chrome and Firefox default `touchstart`, `touchmove` and `wheel` listeners on window, document and body to passive.
- `signal`: an `AbortSignal`. Calling `controller.abort()` removes every listener registered with that signal, which is the cleanest teardown for components.

`removeEventListener` only works with the **same function reference** (and same capture flag). Passing a new inline arrow does nothing.

Custom events: `el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:add", { detail: item, bubbles: true }))`. `dispatchEvent` runs listeners synchronously before it returns.

keyPoints: `querySelectorAll` is a static snapshot; `getElementsBy*` collections are live.
Use `textContent` for untrusted data; `innerHTML` with user input causes XSS.
Batch DOM reads and writes to avoid forced synchronous layout.
Events go capture, target, bubble; listeners default to the bubble phase.
`target` is where the event started; `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running.
`preventDefault` cancels the default action; `stopPropagation` stops travel. They are independent.
Delegation uses one ancestor listener plus `closest()` and handles dynamic children.
Clean up with `AbortController` signals or the same function reference.

questions.prompt: The user clicks the inner element. What is the log order?
questions.explanation: Capture listeners on ancestors run on the way down, before the target. Then the target's listeners run, then bubble listeners on the way up.

questions.prompt: A `<ul>` has a click listener. The user clicks a `<span>` inside an `<li>` in that list. Inside the listener, what are target and currentTarget?
questions.explanation: `target` is the deepest element where the click happened (the span). `currentTarget` is the element the running listener is attached to (the ul).

questions.prompt: The page starts with two .item elements. What is logged?
questions.explanation: `getElementsByClassName` returns a live HTMLCollection that reflects the new element. `querySelectorAll` returns a static NodeList captured at call time.

questions.prompt: The inner listener calls stopPropagation. Which logs appear when inner is clicked?
questions.explanation: stopPropagation stops the event from reaching other elements, so outer's bubble listener never runs. Remaining listeners on the same element still run; only stopImmediatePropagation would skip inner B.

questions.prompt: Why does clicking still call save twice after this code?
options: removeEventListener only works for capture listeners
Each arrow is a different function object, so nothing is removed
Listeners cannot be removed once fired
questions.explanation: removeEventListener matches by function reference (and capture flag). The second arrow is a new function, so it matches nothing. Keep a named reference or use an AbortSignal.

questions.prompt: You need a form-wide handler that reacts when any input inside it gains focus. Which event should the form listen for?
questions.explanation: focus does not bubble, so a listener on the form would not see focus on its inputs (unless using capture). focusin is the bubbling equivalent.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of this code?
questions.code: commentBox.innerHTML = userComment;
options: It is slow because of reflow
Cross-site scripting: user input is parsed as HTML
It throws if comment is empty
questions.explanation: innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so input like `` runs script. Use textContent, or sanitize (for example with DOMPurify) when HTML is required.

questions.prompt: Calling `event.preventDefault()` also stops the event from bubbling.
questions.explanation: preventDefault only cancels the browser's default action. Propagation is controlled separately with stopPropagation.

questions.prompt: `element.dispatchEvent(event)` runs the matching listeners synchronously before it returns.
questions.explanation: Unlike native user events, which are dispatched from tasks, a manual dispatchEvent call invokes listeners immediately, nested inside the calling code.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: benefits of event delegation
options: Works for elements added after setup
Works for events that do not bubble, like focus, without changes
No need to remove listeners from removed children
Guarantees target is the element you care about
questions.explanation: Delegation depends on bubbling, so non-bubbling events need capture or their bubbling equivalents. `event.target` may be a nested descendant, which is why you use closest().

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: call `event.___()` to stop the browser from following a link or submitting a form.
questions.explanation: preventDefault cancels the default action for cancelable events. It is ignored inside passive listeners.

questions.prompt: Explain event bubbling and capturing. When would you use capture?
questions.answer:
- Events travel down from window to the target's parent (capture), run at the target, then travel back up (bubble). Listeners are bubble-phase by default.
- Bubbling is what makes delegation possible: a click on a button can be handled on its container.
- Capture is useful when an ancestor needs to see the event before descendants can stop it: global click-outside detection for menus, analytics, or intercepting events inside third-party widgets that call stopPropagation.
- It is also a way to handle non-bubbling events like focus and blur on a container.
- I'd mention target vs currentTarget, and that stopPropagation in capture on an ancestor prevents the target from ever receiving the event.

questions.prompt: Implement event delegation for a list where items are added dynamically, with a delete button in each item.
questions.answer:
- Attach one click listener on the stable container (the `ul`), not on each button.
- In the handler, find the actual control with `const btn = e.target.closest("[data-action='delete']")`, because the click may hit an icon inside the button.
- Guard: return if btn is null or not inside the container (`e.currentTarget.contains(btn)`).
- Get the item id from a data attribute on the item (`btn.closest("li").dataset.id`) and call the delete logic.
- New items need no extra wiring. When the whole list is torn down, remove the single listener or abort its AbortSignal.
- I'd note keyboard accessibility: use real `<button>` elements so Enter and Space generate click events.

questions.prompt: What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer:
- Browsers batch style and layout work. Reading a geometric property (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, getComputedStyle) when styles are dirty forces the browser to run layout synchronously.
- Interleaving writes and reads in a loop forces a layout per iteration, which can turn a 1 ms update into hundreds of milliseconds and cause jank.
- Avoid it by batching all reads, then all writes; deferring writes to requestAnimationFrame; caching measurements; and using ResizeObserver or IntersectionObserver instead of polling geometry.
- Prefer animating transform and opacity, which can run on the compositor without layout.
- To find it, the Chrome DevTools Performance panel flags "Forced reflow" warnings with the offending call stack.

questions.prompt: How do you make sure event listeners do not leak when a component is destroyed?
questions.answer:
- Track every listener you add to long-lived targets (window, document, a shared element). Listeners on elements you remove are collected with the elements, but listeners on window keep their closures (and everything they reference) alive.
- The simplest pattern is an AbortController per component: pass `{ signal }` to every addEventListener and call `abort()` on teardown.
- Otherwise keep the exact function reference and call removeEventListener with the same capture flag.
- In React, return a cleanup function from useEffect that removes the listener.
- Also clear timers, observers (`observer.disconnect()`) and subscriptions, which leak in the same way. Heap snapshots in DevTools show detached DOM nodes and growing listener counts when something is missed.
